def: A cell secreting a signal that binds receptors on the same cell, rather than on neighbors (paracrine) or distant cells (endocrine). Tumors can use it to drive their own growth.
Progressive self-destruction of an organ by repeated infarcts. In sickle cell disease the spleen shrinks into a fibrotic remnant, leaving patients prone to encapsulated bacterial infections.
A phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitor, like sildenafil, that raises cGMP in penile smooth muscle to treat erectile dysfunction. Contraindicated with nitrates.
A monoclonal antibody against PD-L1, a checkpoint inhibitor used in Merkel cell carcinoma and urothelial cancer.
A beta-lactamase inhibitor combined with ceftazidime to treat resistant gram-negative infections, including carbapenemase-producing (KPC) organisms.
Lack of motivation to start and persist in goal-directed activity, a negative symptom of schizophrenia.
Lysosome-like granules in neutrophils and their precursors that stain purple with Romanowsky dyes and contain myeloperoxidase. Auer rods in acute myeloid leukemia are clumped azurophilic granules.
A lipid carrier in the bacterial membrane that shuttles peptidoglycan building blocks across the cell membrane to the cell wall. Bacitracin blocks its recycling.
Inflammation of the glans penis and foreskin, often from poor hygiene, candida or diabetes in uncircumcised men.
Sinus pain from pressure differences between the sinuses and surrounding air, such as in flying or diving, when the sinus openings are blocked.
An antiprotozoal drug used to treat Chagas disease (Trypanosoma cruzi). Nifurtimox is the alternative.
The toxic metabolite of acetaminophen made by CYP450. Normally detoxified by glutathione, it damages liver cells when glutathione is depleted in overdose. N-acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione.
The herpesvirus subfamily that includes cytomegalovirus (HHV-5) and HHV-6 and HHV-7, which cause roseola.
Involving both copies (alleles) of a gene. Biallelic expression or loss occurs when imprinting is lost or both alleles are mutated.
Stagnation of bile pigment within liver cells and canaliculi seen on biopsy, a sign of cholestasis.
Loud rumbling or gurgling bowel sounds from gas and fluid moving through the intestines, often accentuated in intestinal obstruction.
Infection by Borrelia spirochetes, most commonly Lyme disease from Borrelia burgdorferi spread by Ixodes ticks. Causes erythema migrans, facial palsy, arthritis and carditis.
A forearm muscle that flexes the elbow, tested by the brachioradialis reflex (C5-C6) and innervated by the radial nerve.
The slow-dividing, dormant form of Toxoplasma gondii that forms tissue cysts in muscle and brain. Reactivation in AIDS causes toxoplasmosis encephalitis.
An IV neurosteroid that positively modulates GABA-A receptors. Approved for postpartum depression.
An atypical antipsychotic that is a partial agonist at dopamine D2 and serotonin 5-HT1A receptors. Used for schizophrenia and as add-on in depression.
Production of very large amounts of watery sputum, classically in mucinous adenocarcinoma in situ of the lung.
A perineal muscle that surrounds the base of the penis or the vaginal opening and helps with ejaculation and erection. Innervated by the pudendal nerve.
An industrial chemical used in rubber production. Occupational exposure is linked to leukemia and lymphoma.
A short- to intermediate-acting barbiturate combined with acetaminophen and caffeine for tension headache.
A topical allylamine antifungal that inhibits squalene epoxidase, used for tinea infections.
A newborn foot position with the heel turned outward and the foot sharply flexed upward, caused by cramped positioning in the womb. Usually resolves spontaneously.
Relating to the calyces, the cup-shaped spaces of the kidney that collect urine from the papillae before the renal pelvis. Calyceal dilation indicates hydronephrosis.
A calcium carbonate crystal (otoconium) that has dislodged into a semicircular canal of the inner ear, causing benign paroxysmal positional vertigo.
Widespread genetic damage in a region of tissue from a carcinogen (e.g., sun, smoking), predisposing it to multiple separate premalignant or malignant lesions.
An angiotensin II receptor blocker (ARB) used for hypertension and heart failure. Like other ARBs it is teratogenic and can raise potassium.
Infection with Candida yeasts, causing thrush, vaginitis, esophagitis and, in the immunocompromised, bloodstream disease. Pseudohyphae and budding yeast are seen on microscopy.
Cutting the lateral canthal tendon of the eye, done after canthotomy to relieve pressure in orbital compartment syndrome.
A cut through the outer corner of the eyelids (lateral canthus). Performed emergently to relieve pressure from retrobulbar hemorrhage and prevent blindness.
The final maturation of sperm in the female reproductive tract that enables them to fertilize an egg, including loss of seminal plasma coating and changes in the membrane.
The rounded outer part of the lower end of the humerus that articulates with the radial head at the elbow.
The waveform of exhaled carbon dioxide over time from capnography. A flat line means no exhaled CO2, as with esophageal intubation or cardiac arrest.
Measurement of the carbon dioxide concentration in exhaled breath, usually end-tidal CO2, used to confirm endotracheal tube placement.
Hemoglobin with CO2 bound to its globin amino groups, one way CO2 is carried in blood. Carrying CO2 this way shifts the oxygen curve right (Haldane effect).
A beta-lactamase enzyme that destroys carbapenem antibiotics, making bacteria such as Klebsiella (KPC) multidrug resistant.
A mixture of oxygen and a small percentage of carbon dioxide breathed to cause vasodilation, sometimes used in central retinal artery occlusion.
The red dye in acid-fast (Ziehl-Neelsen, Kinyoun) stains that penetrates the waxy mycolic acid walls of Mycobacterium and Nocardia.
An old term for achalasia, failure of the lower esophageal sphincter to relax with loss of esophageal peristalsis.
Hemorrhagic infarction of a uterine fibroid, also called red degeneration, usually in pregnancy. Causes acute pain and low-grade fever.
The structural protein of caveolae, small membrane pits in cells such as muscle and endothelium. Caveolin-3 mutations cause some limb-girdle muscular dystrophies.
The strip of right atrial tissue between the tricuspid valve and inferior vena cava that carries the reentry circuit of typical atrial flutter. Ablation of it cures flutter.
Surgery to fix the cecum to the abdominal wall, used for cecal volvulus.
A unit of genetic distance equal to a 1% chance of recombination between two gene loci during meiosis.
A pegylated antibody fragment against TNF-alpha, used for Crohn disease and rheumatoid arthritis.
A bivalent HPV vaccine protecting against types 16 and 18, the main causes of cervical cancer.
